overview.description: Piquet is one of the oldest, most sophisticated, and strategically deep card games in Western history. Originating in France as a game for the nobility, it is a two-player trick-taking and melding game played with a 32-card deck. It is celebrated for its 'Rubicon' scoring system and the delicate balance between the 'Elder' and 'Younger' hands. It is a game of skill, psychological maneuvering, and card-counting that has remained unchanged for over 500 years.

history.origins: First mentioned in 1534 in Rabelais' Gargantua and Pantagruel. Legend says it was invented by a knight named Stephen de Vignolles (La Hire) during the reign of Charles VII.
timeline: 1534: First literary mention of the game.
1650s: Becomes the standard game for European aristocrats.
1800s: Widespread in English 'gentlemen's clubs' as a test of intellect.
Present: Declared by Edmond Hoyle as the most scientific of 2-player games.
history.evolution: The'Rubicon' scoring (penalizing a player who fails to reach 100 points) was added to ensure competitive tension throughout all six deals of a match.
history.cultural: Used as a common plot device in 19th-century literature (Jane Austen, Thackeray) to signify character and social standing.

setup.players: Two players only. The non-dealer is the elder hand and the dealer is the younger hand; deal alternates each hand. Players cut for the highest card to decide who deals first (the winner usually chooses to deal first for a slight advantage on the sixth hand). A full game is a partie of six deals.
setup.dealing: Each player receives 12 cards. The remaining 8 cards form the 'Talon' (stock).

rules.objective: Score points through declarations and winning tricks. A game ('Partie') consists of six deals.
rules.gameplay: Deal alternates. Each player receives 12 cards; 8 remain as talon. Non-dealer is elder hand, dealer younger. Carte blanche (no court cards) scores 10 if announced before exchange. Exchange: elder discards 1–5 cards face down and draws the same number from the talon; younger then discards 1 to the remainder and draws the same. Declarations: elder announces best in each category (Point—longest suit; Sequence—tierce to huitième; Set—trio or quatorze). Younger responds good, not good, or equal; only the winner in each category scores. Repique: 30 in declarations before opponent scores any declaration scores 60 extra. Pique: 30 in declarations and play before opponent scores scores 30 extra (only elder can pique). Play: 12 tricks, no trumps, must follow suit. One point per lead; one extra for winning opponent's lead; one for last trick. Majority of tricks scores 10 (the cards); all 12 (capot) scores 40. Partie is six deals; higher total wins. Rubicon: loser under 100 pays sum plus 100; loser 100 or over pays difference plus 100.
keyRules: Elder exchanges first (discard 1–5, draw same from talon); younger then exchanges (1 to remaining cards).
Declarations: Point (longest suit), Sequence (3+ consecutive in suit), Set (trio or quatorze of 10+). Only best in each category scores. Elder declares first.
No trumps. Must follow suit. Highest of led suit wins trick.
Repique: 30 in declarations before opponent scores = 60 bonus. Pique: 30 in declarations+play before opponent = 30 bonus (elder only).
Partie = 6 deals. Winner is higher total. Rubicon scoring applies at end of partie.

strategy.basic: Keep your 'Point'! If you have 5 Spades, do everything to keep them together during the discard phase. A winning Point not only gives you its length in points but also often allows you to sweep the 'Sequence' and 'Quatorze' categories. If you are the Elder, be aggressive with your discardsâ€”you need that Pique/Repique bonus to build a dominant lead.
strategy.intermediate: Counting the Talon: If you are the Younger hand, you only get 3 cards from the talon. However, you are entitled to look at any cards the Elder left behind. Use this information to deduce their hand perfectly. If you know they are missing the King of Diamonds, your Diamond Queen safe to lead.
strategy.advanced: The 'Capot' Risk: If you have an overwhelmingly strong hand, don't just settle for winning 7 tricks. Orchestrate your leads so that the opponent is forced to break their only remaining suit protectors. If you can achieve a 'Capot' (12-0), the 40-point bonus often 'Rubicons' the opponent, doubling your score for the entire match. Piquet is a game of 'Stun and Kill', not just incremental gains.
tips: Always declare 'Carte Blanche' (no face cards) immediately if you have it! It's an instant 10 points.
The Rubicon: If your opponent is at 99 points on the 6th deal, fight like hell to stop them from reaching 100.

difficulty.easy: Makes poor discards; misses Pique/Repique opportunities; doesn't count cards.
difficulty.medium: Excellent at suited point management; basic talon counting; manages Rubicon risk.
difficulty.hard: Expert at 'Information-Asymmetry' play; predicts entire opponent hand after the discard; master of the Capot logic.

phases.label: Exchange
phases.notes: Elder discards 1–5 and draws same from talon; younger then discards 1 to remainder and draws same.

phases.label: Declarations
phases.notes: Elder declares Point, Sequence, Set; younger responds; elder leads first card; younger declares in categories she won or elder did not declare.

phases.label: Play
phases.notes: Twelve tricks; no trumps; must follow suit; trick winner leads next.

declare.description: Announce best combination in each category: Point (longest suit), Sequence (tierce to huitième in one suit), Set (trio or quatorze of 10+). Elder declares first; younger responds good, not good, or equal. Only the winner in each category scores; equal length compared by card values.
declare.constraints: Elder declares before leading; younger declares in categories where she has better or elder did not declare, after elder leads to first trick.

reveal_hand.reason: Hands are not revealed in this phase.

award_pot.reason: This game has no pot to award.

play_card.description: Play one card to the current trick. Must follow suit if possible. No trumps. Each lead scores 1; winning a trick when opponent led scores 1 extra; last trick scores 1. Majority of tricks scores 10 (the cards); all 12 tricks (capot) scores 40.
play_card.constraints: Must follow suit. Highest card of led suit wins trick. Trick winner leads next.

draw.description: During exchange: after discarding, draw the same number of cards from the top of the talon.
draw.constraints: Draw count equals number discarded in the same exchange (elder up to 5, younger up to remainder in talon).

discard.description: During exchange: discard cards face down (elder 1–5, younger 1 to number left in talon), then draw the same number from the top of the talon.
discard.constraints: Elder must discard at least one and at most five; younger at least one and at most the number of cards elder left in the talon.

go_out.reason: This game has no go-out action.

drawSources.notes: After discarding in exchange; draw same number as discarded (elder up to 5, younger up to remainder).

engine.handRankingSystem: Scoring by declarations (Point, Sequence, Set) and by tricks; no trump; highest of led suit wins trick. No poker-style hand ranks.
engine.deckDescription: A 32-card stripped deck: four French suits, ranks 7 through Ace. Classic Piquet: 12 cards each, 8-card talon; exchange, declarations (Point, Sequence, Set), then tricks with no trump; partie of six deals; Rubicon scoring.
engine.suitDescription: The four French suits (hearts, diamonds, clubs, spades) each have eight cards. Declarations use suit and rank; trick play has no trump; highest of led suit wins; card point values apply in declarations and tricks.
engine.rankDescription: Ranks 7 through Ace; Ace is high. Declaration scoring and trick order follow standard Piquet rank values; the talon exchange and declaration phase precede the trick phase in each deal.

scoring.winCondition: Winner of the partie is the player with the higher total after six deals. Rubicon: if loser scored under 100, loser pays sum of scores plus 100; if loser scored 100 or more, loser pays difference plus 100.
